COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (CNN) -- Sri Lanka's government said Monday its forces had killed Tamil rebel chief Velupillai Prabhakaran as he attempted to flee, according to the country's state-run news agency. The Sri Lankan government says Tamil chief Velupillai Prabhakaran is dead. The Tamil rebel group, formally known as the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), is aware of the government's report but has yet to confirm Prabhakaran's death or the deaths of its other leaders, according to a posting on the pro-rebel Web site, Tamilnet.com. It said "initial reports indicate a determined massacre by the Sri Lanka Army." Prabhakaran was one of 19 senior LTTE leaders that the government has identified among the bodies found as its troops completed mop-up operations after routing the Tigers, the defense ministry said. The leaders include Prabhakaran's eldest son, Charles Anthony, as well as Pottu Amman, LTTE's intelligence leader, according to the ministry. Prabhakaran founded the rebel group, which has been declared a terrorist organization by 32 countries. It pioneered the use of women in suicide attacks and, according to the FBI, invented the explosive suicide belt. It was also behind the assassination of two world leaders -- the only terrorist organization to do so.  Watch more on the possible end of fighting » . Prabhakaran is accused of masterminding the killing of former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi in 1991 in the Tamil-dominated Indian state of Tami Nadu as he campaigned for a second term. Sri Lankan authorities allege that Prabhakaran was avenging Gandhi's decision to send Indian peacekeepers to Sri Lanka. Two years later a Tigers suicide bomber, allegedly acting under Prabhakaran's orders, detonated explosives that killed Sri Lanka's then-president, Ranasinghe Premadasa, during a rally. Over the weekend, the militants offered to "silence" their guns after an intense military offensive decimated their ranks, pushed them from their stronghold in the north and east of the country, and cornered the remaining rebels on a small stretch of land. If the rebels honor their pledge, it would potentially mark the end of the longest-running civil war in Asia. Prabhakaran's supporters considered him a hero with a single-minded focus -- to fight for the rights of his people. The Sri Lankan government deemed him a war criminal with a disregard for civilian casualties. He was wanted by Interpol on charges including terrorism and organized crime. In the past it has been reported he wore a cyanide capsule around his neck -- to swallow and kill himself rather than risk capture. And he reportedly expected the same dedication from his troops. As a result, few Tigers have been captured alive. Sri Lanka's President Mahinda Rajapaksa is expected to announce that "military operations" against the Tiger rebels have ended in an address to parliament and country on Tuesday.  Watch aid agencies fear for Sri Lanka » . The rebels have fought for an independent state for minority Tamils in Sri Lanka since July 1983. Journalist Iqbal Athas contributed to this report.

# The Death of Velupillai Prabhakaran and the Fall of the Tamil Tigers

Sri Lanka's state-run news agency reported that government forces had killed Velupillai Prabhakaran, the chief of the Tamil rebel movement, as he attempted to flee the final battle zone. The announcement marked a decisive moment in the country's decades-long civil conflict.

The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), commonly known as the Tamil Tigers, acknowledged the government's report but stopped short of confirming the deaths of Prabhakaran or its other senior leaders. In its response, the organization described the event as a "determined massacre," reflecting its refusal to formally validate the government's account of the leader's demise.

According to the government, Prabhakaran was among 19 senior LTTE leaders whose bodies were identified in the aftermath of the fighting. Among the deceased were several key figures in the movement, including his eldest son, Charles Anthony, and the group's intelligence chief, Pottu Amman.

The LTTE, which had been designated a terrorist organization by 32 countries, was notorious for its ruthless and innovative tactics. The group pioneered the use of women in suicide attacks and is widely credited with inventing the explosive suicide belt, a device that would later be adopted by militant organizations around the world.

Prabhakaran himself was accused of masterminding some of the most high-profile political assassinations in South Asian history. These included the killing of Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi in 1991 and the assassination of Sri Lankan President Ranasinghe Premadasa in 1993, acts that cemented his reputation as one of the region's most feared insurgent leaders.

**Sri Lanka Announces Death of Tamil Tiger Chief Prabhakaran, Signaling End to Decades-Long Conflict**

The Sri Lankan government announced on Monday that its armed forces had killed Velupillai Prabhakaran, the elusive founder and supreme leader of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), during mop-up operations conducted in the aftermath of the military's comprehensive routing of the rebel movement. According to official statements, Prabhakaran was killed alongside 18 other senior members of the rebel leadership as government troops swept through the last remaining sliver of territory that had been under Tiger control in the island nation's northeast.

The announcement marks what may be a decisive and historic turning point in one of Asia's longest-running armed conflicts, a civil war that had raged for more than a quarter of a century and claimed the lives of tens of thousands of people. Government forces had, in recent weeks and months, steadily reduced the once-formidable rebel-held region to a tiny coastal enclave, gradually cornering the fighters and eventually overwhelming their remaining positions.

Despite the government's confident assertions, the LTTE itself had not yet confirmed the death of its leader, leaving a measure of uncertainty hanging over the dramatic developments. The rebel organization, known for its secrecy and discipline, had a history of both surviving apparent setbacks and defying reports of its demise, and observers noted that independent verification of the claims remained difficult given the tightly controlled nature of the conflict zone.

Prabhakaran, who had led the Tigers since founding the group in the 1970s, was one of the world's most wanted and feared insurgent leaders. Over the course of his long insurgency, he built the LTTE into a highly organized fighting force that pioneered the use of suicide bombers and maintained its own naval and air capabilities, an extraordinary feat for a non-state armed group. His stated goal was the creation of an independent homeland for Sri Lanka's Tamil minority, a cause he pursued with unrelenting militancy.

He was accused of orchestrating a campaign of political violence that reached far beyond Sri Lanka's borders, including the assassinations of two world leaders. Among the most notorious of these was the 1991 killing of former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi, carried out by a female suicide bomber, an act that fundamentally altered India's relationship with the Tamil cause. Under his command, the LTTE came to be formally designated as a terrorist organization by at least 32 countries, including major powers such as the United States, the United Kingdom, and India.

With the reported death of Prabhakaran and the collapse of the Tiger leadership, the Sri Lankan government appeared poised to declare a definitive military victory, potentially bringing to an end a brutal conflict that had shaped the nation's politics and society for generations. Yet even as celebrations were anticipated among government supporters, questions loomed over the humanitarian toll of the final offensive, the fate of civilians caught in the fighting, and the prospects for lasting reconciliation between the country's Sinhalese majority and Tamil minority in the war's aftermath.

# Colombo: The Vibrant Heart of Sri Lanka

Colombo stands as the largest city and commercial capital of Sri Lanka, a captivating island nation located in the Indian Ocean off the southern coast of India. As the country's bustling economic center, Colombo serves as a fascinating gateway to the rich culture, history, and natural beauty that Sri Lanka has to offer.

## A City of Contrasts

Colombo beautifully blends the old with the new. Modern skyscrapers and shopping complexes rise alongside colonial-era buildings, ancient temples, and traditional markets. This unique combination reflects the city's diverse heritage, shaped by centuries of trade and various colonial influences from the Portuguese, Dutch, and British.

## Historical Significance

Throughout its history, Colombo has been an important port city due to its strategic location along ancient trade routes. Merchants from across the world once traveled here to trade spices, particularly cinnamon, which grew abundantly in the region. Today, remnants of this colonial past can be seen in landmarks scattered throughout the city.

## Cultural Diversity

One of Colombo's most remarkable features is its cultural and religious diversity. The city is home to Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims, and Christians who live together harmoniously. This diversity is reflected in the numerous places of worship, including magnificent temples, mosques, and churches that dot the urban landscape.

## Attractions and Experiences

Visitors to Colombo can explore:

- **Galle Face Green**: A scenic oceanfront promenade perfect for evening strolls
- **Gangaramaya Temple**: A stunning Buddhist temple with intricate architecture
- **National Museum**: Showcasing Sri Lanka's rich history and heritage
- **Pettah Market**: A vibrant bazaar offering everything from textiles to spices
- **Colombo Fort**: The historic and business district of the city

## Conclusion

Colombo represents the dynamic spirit of Sri Lanka, offering visitors an authentic experience of this beautiful island nation. Whether you're interested in history, culture, cuisine, or simply soaking in the tropical atmosphere, Colombo provides a memorable introduction to the wonders of Sri Lanka.

# Sri Lankan Government Announces Death of Tamil Tiger Leader Prabhakaran

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka** — Sri Lankan government forces announced the death of Velupillai Prabhakaran, the elusive founder and leader of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), marking a potential end to one of Asia's longest-running and most brutal civil conflicts.

Government officials said Prabhakaran was killed as military forces overran the last remaining pocket of rebel-held territory in the country's northeast. State television broadcast images that officials said confirmed the death of the man who had led the separatist insurgency for more than three decades.

## A Feared and Enigmatic Leader

Prabhakaran, believed to be in his mid-50s, was one of the world's most wanted men, sought by Interpol and designated a terrorist by more than 30 countries. He founded the LTTE in 1976 with the goal of creating an independent Tamil homeland in the north and east of the island nation.

Known for his ruthless discipline and secretive lifestyle, Prabhakaran built the Tamil Tigers into one of the most sophisticated and heavily armed insurgent groups in the world. The organization pioneered the use of suicide bombers, developing an elite unit known as the Black Tigers, and was among the first militant groups to deploy female fighters in significant numbers.

## Background on the Conflict

The roots of the conflict trace back to ethnic tensions between Sri Lanka's Sinhalese majority, who are predominantly Buddhist, and the Tamil minority, largely Hindu, who make up roughly 12 percent of the population. Many Tamils felt marginalized by government policies following the country's independence from Britain in 1948, particularly measures affecting language rights and access to education and employment.

The civil war erupted in 1983 following anti-Tamil riots that killed hundreds and displaced thousands. Over the following decades, the fighting claimed an estimated 70,000 to 100,000 lives and displaced hundreds of thousands more.

At the height of their power, the Tamil Tigers controlled vast swaths of territory, operating a de facto state complete with their own police force, courts, and taxation system. They possessed a naval wing known as the Sea Tigers and even a rudimentary air force.

## Notable Attacks

The LTTE was linked to several high-profile assassinations during the conflict, including the 1991 killing of former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi by a female suicide bomber, and the 1993 assassination of Sri Lankan President Ranasinghe Premadasa.

## The Final Offensive

The government's military campaign intensified dramatically after the collapse of a Norwegian-brokered ceasefire that had been signed in 2002. Government forces launched a sustained offensive that steadily reduced rebel-held territory.

The final phase of fighting drew international concern over the fate of tens of thousands of civilians trapped in the shrinking conflict zone. Humanitarian organizations and foreign governments repeatedly called for measures to protect noncombatants caught between the two sides.

## An Uncertain Future

While the death of Prabhakaran and the military defeat of the LTTE mark a significant turning point, analysts caution that Sri Lanka faces substantial challenges ahead. Questions remain about reconciliation between the country's ethnic communities, the resettlement of displaced civilians, and addressing the underlying grievances that fueled the decades of conflict.

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

---

*Note: This article is written in a historical CNN-style format. The events described took place in May 2009.*

# LTTE Leadership Eliminated as Sri Lanka Declares End to Decades-Long Civil War

*By International Wire Service*

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka** — The Sri Lankan government declared victory in its 26-year civil war after security forces killed the leader of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) and virtually the entire senior rebel command, bringing a bloody end to one of Asia's longest-running insurgencies.

Velupillai Prabhakaran, the elusive founder and supreme leader of the Tamil Tigers, was killed as government troops overran the last sliver of rebel-held territory in the northeast of the island nation, military officials confirmed. His death marks the collapse of a separatist movement that had at its height controlled vast swathes of the country and operated a de facto state with its own police, courts, and military.

## The Final Offensive

Government forces cornered the remaining rebel fighters in a narrow coastal strip, an area that had shrunk dramatically over months of relentless military pressure. The military reported that Prabhakaran was killed along with several top lieutenants, including senior military and intelligence commanders who had formed the backbone of the organization's leadership for decades.

Among those reported killed were the group's political wing leader, its intelligence chief, and Prabhakaran's own son, who commanded an elite fighting unit. State television broadcast images intended to confirm the deaths of the rebel commanders.

President Mahinda Rajapaksa, addressing the nation, proclaimed that Sri Lanka had been "liberated from terrorism" and that the country could finally begin a new chapter of unity and reconciliation.

## A War of Attrition

The conflict, which erupted in 1983, claimed an estimated 80,000 to 100,000 lives over its course. The LTTE fought to carve out an independent homeland for the country's Tamil minority in the north and east, citing decades of political and economic marginalization by the Sinhalese-majority government.

The Tigers gained international notoriety for pioneering the use of suicide bombers—including the assassination of former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi in 1991 and Sri Lankan President Ranasinghe Premadasa in 1993. The group was designated a terrorist organization by numerous governments, including the United States, the European Union, and India.

## Humanitarian Concerns

The final months of the offensive drew sharp criticism from international observers and human rights organizations, who raised alarm over the fate of tens of thousands of civilians trapped in the war zone. Aid agencies reported heavy casualties among non-combatants caught in the crossfire, and the United Nations expressed grave concern over conditions in the conflict area.

The government restricted independent access to the war zone, making casualty figures difficult to verify. Rights groups called for an investigation into alleged violations by both the military and the rebels, who were accused of using civilians as human shields.

Hundreds of thousands of displaced Tamil civilians were held in government-run camps, raising questions about resettlement and their long-term welfare.

## An Uncertain Peace

While the military defeat of the LTTE ended active hostilities, analysts cautioned that the underlying grievances that fueled the conflict remained unresolved. The challenge of achieving genuine reconciliation between the Sinhalese and Tamil communities—and addressing longstanding Tamil demands for greater autonomy and equal rights—loomed large over the government's declaration of victory.

International governments urged Colombo to pursue a political solution that would address the concerns of the Tamil population and ensure the humanitarian needs of those displaced by the fighting were met.

For a nation scarred by more than a quarter-century of violence, the guns had fallen silent. Whether a lasting peace could take root remained the defining question of the post-war era.

*— With reporting from Colombo and regional bureaus.*

# Sri Lankan Military Declares Victory Over Tamil Tigers; Rebel Leader Prabhakaran Reported Dead

## Decades-Long Civil War Reaches Bloody Conclusion in Northern Sri Lanka

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka** — The Sri Lankan government declared a decisive military victory over the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), effectively ending one of Asia's longest-running civil conflicts, following the reported death of the rebel group's elusive founder and leader, Velupillai Prabhakaran.

Military officials announced that Prabhakaran was killed as government forces overran the last sliver of territory held by the Tigers in the northeastern coastal region. State television broadcast images purported to show the leader's body, and Army Commander Lieutenant General Sarath Fonseka declared the country "liberated from terrorism."

President Mahinda Rajapaksa, addressing the nation, proclaimed the dawn of a new era. "We have won this battle," he said. "We have liberated the whole country from the clutches of terrorism."

## The Final Offensive

The government's victory came after months of intensive fighting that gradually squeezed the once-formidable rebel force into an ever-shrinking pocket of land along the northeastern coast. In the final weeks, tens of thousands of civilians remained trapped in the conflict zone, prompting international alarm over the humanitarian toll.

Government forces captured the LTTE's administrative capital of Kilinochchi earlier in the campaign, a symbolic blow to a group that had for years administered a de facto state across broad swaths of the north and east. As the military advanced, the rebels lost access to their strongholds and were pushed toward the Indian Ocean.

Humanitarian organizations, including the United Nations, expressed grave concern over civilian casualties during the offensive, with estimates of the dead and displaced running into the tens of thousands. Both the government and the rebels faced accusations of endangering non-combatants—the military for shelling densely populated areas, and the Tigers for allegedly using civilians as human shields and preventing their escape.

## Who Was Velupillai Prabhakaran?

Born in 1954 in Velvettithurai, a coastal town in the Jaffna Peninsula, Prabhakaran founded the LTTE in 1976, transforming a small militant outfit into one of the world's most sophisticated and feared insurgent organizations.

A reclusive figure who rarely appeared in public, Prabhakaran built the Tigers into a disciplined fighting force complete with its own army, navy (the "Sea Tigers"), and a nascent air wing. He was known for demanding absolute loyalty; members reportedly wore cyanide capsules around their necks to swallow if captured, ensuring they could not be interrogated.

Prabhakaran's stated goal was the creation of an independent Tamil homeland, called Tamil Eelam, in the north and east of Sri Lanka. He justified the armed struggle as a response to decades of discrimination against the island's Tamil minority by the Sinhalese-majority government.

## Roots of the Conflict

The Sri Lankan civil war has deep ethnic and political origins. The island nation's population is predominantly Sinhalese and Buddhist, while Tamils—largely Hindu—constitute a significant minority concentrated in the north and east.

Following independence from Britain in 1948, many Tamils felt marginalized by policies that favored the Sinhalese majority, including the "Sinhala Only" language act of 1956 and university admission standards that Tamils viewed as discriminatory. Rising tensions erupted into periodic communal violence, culminating in the anti-Tamil riots of July 1983—known as "Black July"—in which hundreds, possibly thousands, of Tamils were killed. That episode is widely regarded as the trigger for full-scale war.

## A History of Terror

Over more than a quarter-century of conflict, the LTTE earned a reputation for ruthless tactics that led more than 30 countries, including the United States, the European Union, and India, to designate it a terrorist organization.

The group is credited with pioneering the modern suicide bombing as a systematic weapon of war. Its elite suicide unit, the Black Tigers, carried out numerous devastating attacks.

Among the most infamous incidents attributed to the LTTE:

- **The 1991 assassination of former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi**, killed by a female suicide bomber at a campaign rally in Tamil Nadu, in apparent retaliation for India's earlier military intervention in the conflict.

- **The 1993 assassination of Sri Lankan President Ranasinghe Premadasa**, also by a suicide bomber.

- **The 1996 bombing of the Central Bank in Colombo**, which killed around 90 people and injured more than 1,400.

- Numerous attacks on civilian, religious, and infrastructure targets, including the bombing of the Temple of the Tooth in Kandy, one of Buddhism's holiest sites, and assaults on the Bandaranaike International Airport.

The group was also condemned internationally for its recruitment of child soldiers and for the assassination of moderate Tamil politicians and rival leaders, including the killing of its own eastern commander who defected to the government.

## Failed Peace Efforts

Multiple attempts to end the conflict through negotiation collapsed over the years. A Norwegian-brokered ceasefire in 2002 raised hopes for a lasting peace, but the truce gradually unraveled amid mutual accusations of violations. The government formally withdrew from the ceasefire agreement in early 2008, setting the stage for the final military campaign.

## An Uncertain Peace

While the government's military triumph marks the end of organized armed resistance by the Tigers, analysts caution that lasting peace will depend on addressing the underlying grievances that fueled the insurgency. Questions remain over the resettlement of displaced civilians, reconciliation between communities, and the extent to which Tamil political aspirations will be accommodated within a unified Sri Lanka.

International human rights organizations have called for independent investigations into alleged abuses committed by both sides during the war's final stages, and for accountability regarding civilian casualties.

For now, the streets of Colombo and other Sinhalese-majority areas erupted in celebration, with jubilant crowds waving national flags and setting off fireworks. Yet in the war-ravaged north, the population faces the daunting task of rebuilding shattered lives in the aftermath of a conflict that claimed an estimated 70,000 to 100,000 lives over 26 years.

Whether this military victory can be transformed into a durable and inclusive peace remains the central question confronting Sri Lanka as it emerges from the shadow of one of the modern era's most brutal civil wars.

---

# Sri Lankan Government Claims Rebel Leader Prabhakaran Killed in Final Offensive

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka** — The Sri Lankan government announced today that Velupillai Prabhakaran, the elusive founder and leader of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), was killed as he attempted to flee advancing military forces in the northeastern coastal region, marking what officials describe as the definitive end to one of Asia's longest-running armed conflicts.

## The Government's Account

Military officials stated that Prabhakaran died during a final assault on the shrinking pocket of rebel-held territory in the country's northeast. According to army sources, the rebel leader was killed while trying to escape the combat zone in a vehicle, alongside several senior lieutenants.

"The military operation to liberate the country from terrorism has reached its conclusion," a senior government spokesman told reporters, adding that the recovery of the body was being verified through multiple identification methods.

State television broadcast triumphant announcements, and celebratory scenes erupted in parts of Colombo, where residents set off firecrackers and waved national flags.

## Rebel Response

In a statement attributed to the LTTE's international relations chief, the organization offered a contradictory account, at one point suggesting their leader remained "alive and safe." The conflicting claims from rebel sources reflected the chaos of the conflict's closing chapter, as the group's communications infrastructure lay in disarray following weeks of military encirclement.

The LTTE, which for decades maintained sophisticated propaganda operations, appeared unable to mount a unified response to the government's declaration.

## A Conflict Spanning Decades

The armed struggle, which began in the 1980s, sought to establish an independent homeland for the country's Tamil minority in the north and east. The conflict claimed tens of thousands of lives over more than a quarter-century and drew international concern over the humanitarian toll, particularly regarding civilians trapped in the final battle zones.

Prabhakaran, who founded the movement as a young man, had become one of the world's most wanted figures, with the LTTE designated a terrorist organization by numerous nations.

## Questions Ahead

While the government framed the day as a moment of national triumph, aid organizations and international observers cautioned that significant challenges remain. Humanitarian groups highlighted the plight of displaced civilians who fled the fighting, and analysts raised questions about long-term reconciliation between the country's ethnic communities.

Whether the death of the rebel leadership brings a lasting peace—or leaves unresolved the underlying grievances that fueled the insurgency—remains among the most pressing questions facing the nation as it emerges from years of war.
